name.text: Determining tangent using the unit circle

questiontext.text:
The angle \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\) is in standard position: it is measured anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. Its terminal side meets the unit circle (centre \(O\), radius \(1\)) at the point \(P\), as shown in the diagram.

Use the unit circle to find the exact value of \(\tan\theta\). Recall that \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

The point \(P\) on the unit circle has coordinates \((\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)\), so \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{y}{x}\). We find \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) from the reference angle and the quadrant, then divide.

Step 1: find the quadrant and the reference angle. \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\) lies in Quadrant {@quadname@}. [[if test="is(quadrant=1)"]]It is already acute, so the reference angle is \(\alpha = \theta = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quadrant=2)"]]The reference angle is \(\alpha = 180^\circ - \theta = 180^\circ - {@theta@}^\circ = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quadrant=3)"]]The reference angle is \(\alpha = \theta - 180^\circ = {@theta@}^\circ - 180^\circ = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(quadrant=4)"]]The reference angle is \(\alpha = 360^\circ - \theta = 360^\circ - {@theta@}^\circ = {@ref_angle@}^\circ\).[[/if]]

Step 2: use the exact values for the reference angle. From the special triangles,

\[ \sin {@ref_angle@}^\circ = {@sin_ref@}, \qquad \cos {@ref_angle@}^\circ = {@cos_ref@}. \]

Step 3: give each value its sign. In Quadrant {@quadname@}, \(P\) is [[if test="is(quadrant=1 or quadrant=4)"]]to the right of the \(y\)-axis, so \(\cos\theta\) is positive,[[else]]to the left of the \(y\)-axis, so \(\cos\theta\) is negative,[[/if]] and [[if test="is(quadrant=1 or quadrant=2)"]]above the \(x\)-axis, so \(\sin\theta\) is positive.[[else]]below the \(x\)-axis, so \(\sin\theta\) is negative.[[/if]] So

\[ \sin {@theta@}^\circ = {@sin_theta@}, \qquad \cos {@theta@}^\circ = {@cos_theta@}. \]

Step 4: divide.

\[ \tan {@theta@}^\circ = \frac{\sin {@theta@}^\circ}{\cos {@theta@}^\circ} = \dfrac{ {@sin_theta@} }{ {@cos_theta@} }. \]

[[if test="is(quadrant=1 or quadrant=3)"]]The sine and cosine have the same sign, so \(\tan\theta\) is positive.[[else]]The sine and cosine have opposite signs, so \(\tan\theta\) is negative.[[/if]] For the size, divide the values for the reference angle: [[if test="is(ref_angle=30)"]]\(\dfrac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(ref_angle=45)"]]\(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}/2}{\sqrt{2}/2} = 1\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(ref_angle=60)"]]\(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}/2}{1/2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{1} = \sqrt{3}\).[[/if]] Therefore

\[ \tan {@theta@}^\circ = {@tan_theta@}[[if test="is(ref_angle=30)"]] = [[if test="is(tsign=1)"]]\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}[[else]]-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}[[/if]][[/if]]. \]

Seeing \(\tan\theta\) on the unit circle. Since \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{x}\), it is the gradient of the line \(OP\). In the diagram, the line through \(O\) and \(P\) meets the vertical tangent line \(x = 1\) at \(T = (1,\, \tan\theta)\). The green length from the \(x\)-axis up (or down) to \(T\) is \(\tan\theta\).[[if test="is(quadrant=2 or quadrant=3)"]] Here \(P\) is on the left of the \(y\)-axis, so the line has to be extended back through \(O\) to reach \(x = 1\).[[/if]]

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: The size of your answer is right, but the sign is wrong. In which quadrant is \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\)? Decide the signs of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) there: \(\tan\theta\) is positive when they have the same sign and negative when they have opposite signs.
It looks as if you have divided the wrong way round. \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\): the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\) divided by its \(x\)-coordinate.

falsefeedback.text: Find the reference angle and the exact values of its sine and cosine. Use the quadrant of \(\theta\) to give each one its sign, then divide \(\sin\theta\) by \(\cos\theta\).
